word:lxx:L700035.explanation: This is a proper name, rendered “Abdōn” or “Avthon,” used to identify a person rather than describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Judges and once in 2 Chronicles. The available references preserve the name, but no surrounding verse text is provided here, so the broader significance of each occurrence cannot be stated from the name alone. Its basic meaning is the personal name Abdōn, also rendered Avthon.

word:lxx:L700079.explanation: Abital is a personal name, rendered “Abital” or “Avital.” It functions as the name of a particular person rather than as a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: in 2 Samuel 3:4 and 1 Chronicles 3:3. The available wording identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in either passage.

word:lxx:L700097.explanation: Abrōtos means uneatable or not good for food.

word:lxx:L700123.explanation: This word means “loving” and, as a noun, names the quality or expression of being loving. It refers to love as a recognizable attitude or disposition rather than functioning as an action word. In the Greek Old Testament, including its deuterocanonical books, it occurs 17 times in 16 verses. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains loving concern directed toward another.

word:lxx:L700156.explanation: This noun refers to a “holy place” or “sanctuary”—a place set apart as sacred. In the Greek Old Testament, it names a sacred location, not merely a quality of holiness. The word occurs four times, appearing once in Leviticus and three times in Psalms. Its precise reference in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a holy place or sanctuary.

word:lxx:L700394.explanation: Aingadois, also rendered Enggathis, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek text, but the available information does not establish which one. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Sirach 24:14. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from that passage’s surrounding context and the wider biblical setting.

word:lxx:L700440.explanation: Ailōm, also rendered Elom, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, across three verses in Joshua and Judges. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not identify whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise referent therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the specific biblical context.

word:lxx:L700527.explanation: Akatan is a personal name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek text, in Ezra 8:12. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the person’s role and the significance of the name in that passage cannot be explained further from this word alone. Its basic meaning, therefore, is simply the proper name Akatan.

word:lxx:L700585.explanation: This LXX verb means “make to hear,” describing an action that brings someone or something into hearing. It is a verb, so it expresses what is done rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, across passages in Judges, Psalms, Jeremiah, Sirach, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L700606.explanation: This adjective describes something at the highest or most prominent point—the “pinnacle” or “apex.” It can identify a chief, elevated position rather than something ordinary or low. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 28:16. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea is a prominent topmost point or leading position.

word:lxx:L700754.explanation: The word is the proper name “Amathar.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Joshua 19:13. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name’s particular referent cannot be identified more precisely from this lexical entry alone. The entry preserves only the name itself, not an extended definition or description.

word:lxx:L700978.explanation: “Impede” means to hinder or hold something back so that it cannot move forward freely. As a verb, this word describes an action that interferes with progress rather than simply naming a fixed condition. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times: once in Wisdom and twice in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what is being hindered, but its central idea remains preventing or slowing progress.

word:lxx:L701142.explanation: This adjective describes someone who has not yet reached manhood, or who is still beardless. It points to an immature male in terms of age or physical development, rather than expressing a moral judgment. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:13. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the description functions there, but its basic meaning is a male who has not yet come to man’s estate.

word:lxx:L701230.explanation: This verb means “write against”: it describes putting something into writing in opposition or response to what has already been written. As a verb, it names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 1 Maccabees. The precise force of the action in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L701393.explanation: This adjective describes something that cannot be brought to an end—something interminable. It presents duration, extent, or continuation as having no clear stopping point, rather than merely lasting a long time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines what continuing or unending thing is being described.

word:lxx:L701403.explanation: “Hatefully” describes an action, attitude, or manner carried out with hatred or strong hostility. As an adverb, it tells how someone speaks, treats another person, or acts, rather than naming the person or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom 19:15 and 3 Maccabees 5:3. Without the surrounding verse text, its exact force in either passage cannot be explained further, but its basic sense is clear: something is done in a hateful, hostile way.

word:lxx:L701476.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “laid away” or “reserved,” describing something set aside or kept for a later purpose. It can refer to something placed in readiness rather than used immediately. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise force depends on the sentence where it occurs. It is found in Genesis, Job, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees.

word:lxx:L701519.explanation: This adjective describes something that remains after other things have been removed, used, or accounted for—what is left over or left behind. It can refer to a remaining portion, space, or part rather than to something newly added. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times, all in Ezekiel, especially in the detailed descriptions of the temple and its surrounding areas. Its precise reference depends on the noun or place being described in each sentence.

word:lxx:L701612.explanation: Apotēganizō means to broil or cook.

word:lxx:L701708.explanation: This verb means “coin money”—to produce or mint money. It describes the act of making coins rather than simply possessing, counting, or spending them. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 6:29. Because no verse text is included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its surrounding context; its basic lexical sense remains the making of money. The word is an action word, focusing attention on the work of producing coined currency.

word:lxx:L701771.explanation: Armaith is a proper name, rendered “Armaith,” with “Armeth” given as an alternate form. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 19:36. Because it is a name rather than a common noun or action word, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it designates a particular named entity in that passage. The available information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything more specific about the name’s referent.

word:lxx:L701810.explanation: This adjective describes something that is “without roots” or “uprooted”—no longer firmly planted or established. It can refer to a plant that has been pulled from the ground, or more generally to something deprived of its foundation. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Job 31:8, and its translated rendering there is “uprooted.” The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely how the image functions in that passage.

word:lxx:L701964.explanation: This verb means to “endeavor”: to make a deliberate effort toward something. That reference identifies where the word appears, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the particular situation. Its basic sense remains focused on active effort or earnest attempt.

word:lxx:L702020.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “anklebone,” the bony joint connecting the foot and lower leg. It names a specific part of the body rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a literal reference to the anklebone.

word:lxx:L702169.explanation: This word means “neck” or “throat,” referring to the part of the body between the head and shoulders. It is a noun used for this bodily area, whether described as a single neck or as necks. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Joshua, 2 Chronicles, Psalms, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:lxx:L702187.explanation: Apharsaioi, also rendered Afarsei, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. word:lxx:L702213.explanation: This noun means “departure,” referring to the act of leaving or going away. word:lxx:L702341.explanation: Baalia, also rendered Vaalia, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L702402.explanation: Baithacharma, also rendered Vethakharma, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. word:lxx:L702644.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “missile.” It refers to a weapon sent toward a target, such as something launched or thrown in battle. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a missile used against a target.

word:lxx:L702688.explanation: “Bēthleem; Vithleem” is a proper name for the place known in English as Bethlehem. word:lxx:L703052.explanation: Gennēma means spawn or offspring. It can also mean the produce or fruit yielded by land.

word:lxx:L703236.explanation: Dabirōn is a proper name, also given as “Thaviron.” It is not presented as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament. word:lxx:L703243.explanation: Daemia, also rendered Thaemia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, but the available lexical information supports treating it as a name, not translating it as an ordinary descriptive term.

word:lxx:L703315.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “coward”: it describes acting with cowardice or shrinking back from courage. word:lxx:L703445.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “bind round”: to wrap or fasten something around another object. It describes an action rather than a person, place, or quality. word:lxx:L703683.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “extend”: to reach or stretch outward or onward. It describes an action rather than a person or object. word:lxx:L703777.explanation: This noun means “evaluation”—the act of examining or assessing something to determine its quality, fitness, or worth. word:lxx:L703799.explanation: This adjective describes someone captured in battle—a “captive of the spear” or one “taken in war.” It portrays a person who has been seized as a result of armed conflict, rather than someone who freely chooses a situation. word:lxx:L704196.explanation: This adjective describes something “out of law,” “lawless,” or “horrible.” It identifies conduct or a thing as outside what is lawful and therefore morally disturbing or dreadful. word:lxx:L704264.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “vanish”: to disappear or pass out of sight. It describes an action rather than a person or object, telling what someone or something does. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains disappearance.

word:lxx:L704310.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “scare away”: to frighten someone or something so that it retreats or goes off. word:lxx:L704453.explanation: Eliatha is a proper name referring to a person named Eliatha. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 25:27. word:lxx:L704534.explanation: Elymais, also rendered Elimes, is a proper name for a place or region. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Daniel 8:2 and once in 1 Maccabees 6:1. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is the place-name Elymais.

word:lxx:L704581.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “mockery”—words or actions that ridicule, scorn, or make a person or thing seem foolish. It names an expression of derision rather than a neutral statement. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, once in Isaiah and once in Wisdom, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in either passage depends on the context in which the mockery appears.

word:lxx:L704611.explanation: Emporeuomai means to do business, or trade.

word:lxx:L704668.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “let drop into”: it describes allowing something to fall or be lowered into a place. As a verb, it expresses an action or permission rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Ezekiel 21:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the act of letting something drop into a specified place.

word:lxx:L704893.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to “slip out”—to get away or leave quietly. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish Scripture represented here, once in Job and once in Sirach. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic idea remains a quiet or unnoticed departure. The word is therefore best understood as an action of escaping, leaving, or getting free without drawing attention.

word:lxx:L704930.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to “reach” or “arrive at” a place or destination. It describes coming as far as a particular point, emphasizing arrival rather than merely setting out or traveling. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Judges 5:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is movement that successfully comes to a designated place.

word:lxx:L705047.explanation: This verb describes breathing hard—panting while engaged in strenuous work. It refers to the physical act of laboring with force or exertion, not to a broad feeling or abstract idea. Its basic meaning is “breathe hard; pant in working.” In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:11. The word therefore presents a vivid physical picture of someone breathing heavily during demanding labor.

word:lxx:L705102.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “impose as a burden”—to place a load, responsibility, or demand upon someone. The precise force of that occurrence belongs to its surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s basic meaning is to burden or load someone with an imposed demand.

word:lxx:L705270.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “prop up” or “steady”: it describes giving support so that someone or something is held firm rather than left to fall or waver. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing across books such as Genesis, Judges, 2 Samuel, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom it describes.

word:lxx:L705292.explanation: This verb means to trouble— to cause difficulty, disturbance, or distress. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:24. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of troubling. word:lxx:L705388.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “labour” or “work”: effort or activity undertaken to accomplish something. word:lxx:L705425.explanation: This noun refers to a day-labourer or hired servant: someone engaged to work for pay. word:lxx:L705469.explanation: Esdrikam, also rendered Ezthrikam, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L705487.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to “Esthaōlaioi; Esthaolei.” It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word or action, but as the name of a particular group or designation. word:lxx:L705520.explanation: Eschōl, also rendered Eskhol, is a proper name used for a person or place identified by that name. word:lxx:L705638.explanation: This adjective describes something musical or rhythmical—marked by pleasing sound, ordered movement, or a harmonious quality. The word focuses on the character of a sound or movement rather than naming a person, action, or object by itself. Its exact force in that verse depends on the sentence where it occurs.

word:lxx:L705641.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something that is well-disposed or favourable. word:lxx:L705713.explanation: This verb means to “use words of good omen”—to speak in a way associated with favorable signs or wishes. word:lxx:L705766.explanation: Ephrathaios is a proper name, also given as “Efratheos.” It is a name used in the Greek Old Testament rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L705814.explanation: This proper noun identifies a person called a “Zaboulōnitēs,” also rendered “Zavulonitis.” It functions as a personal or group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L705933.explanation: This noun means “command”—an authoritative direction or order given to someone. word:lxx:L705946.explanation: Hēdysma means something that gives a relish.

word:lxx:L706114.explanation: Tharthak is a proper name, referring to a specific figure or deity named in the Greek Old Testament. word:lxx:L706262.explanation: This verb means “touch”: to make contact with someone or something. word:lxx:L706280.explanation: Thoada, also known as Thoatha, is a personal name rather than a descriptive word. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles chapter 4.
